Fixed for real this time — and I can tell you exactly why every previous fix was structurally incapable of working.

## The root cause we kept missing

Our rescue handlers listened on `vite:preloadError` and `unhandledrejection`. But I read VitePress's router source: **it catches the failed page import itself**, inside `loadPage`'s own try/catch. The error never reaches either channel. VitePress then refetches `hashmap.json`, retries, and either renders its not-found fallback or pulls *new* chunks into the *old* running app and breaks the render. Blank page, zero signals fired. We were installing smoke detectors in a room the fire never enters.

## The fix: prevent, don't rescue

New `deploy-guard.ts`, wired into `onBeforeRouteChange` (which is awaited and cancelable):

- Every built page inlines its own `__VP_HASH_MAP__`; the server serves the current one at `/hashmap.json` with `max-age=0`. Navigation breaks **exactly when those two disagree** — so that comparison is the whole test, no build-id infrastructure needed.
- Before any SPA navigation (throttled — a fresh verdict holds 30s): if the maps disagree, cancel the SPA hop and `location.assign` — a full page load onto the new build. Compared against the map **snapshotted at boot**, because VitePress overwrites the live global during its retry.
- Tab refocus and bfcache restore run the check in the background, so a tab left open overnight is already armed before you click.
- Fails open on network trouble — offline reading keeps working. Old handlers stay as backstop, and a not-found page now reloads when the maps disagree (stale-build "404"s aren't real 404s).

## Proven, not assumed

I reproduced the actual race live: held a tab open on ivue.dev, ran a real deploy underneath it, clicked Blog. First run exposed two things — a quick A/B test can *false-pass* because old immutable-cached chunks linger at the edge (which is why this bug always dodged our tests), and my initial 800ms check timeout could fail open. Bumped to 2.5s, instrumented, re-ran: the stale tab logged `[deploy-guard] new deploy detected`, the click became a verified **full reload** (a probe variable I planted was wiped), and the blog rendered.

If any tab ever misbehaves again, open its console and run `__ivueDeployGuard.state()` — it reports the last check's outcome, so we debug from evidence instead of guessing. Comparing local *dates* rather than raw hours avoids drift (a send at 9:03 never pushes the next one to 10am two days later). DST comes free with IANA zones via `Intl` in the Worker.

Built, tested, deployed, and verified live. Your next email: **`twenty-million-cells`, tomorrow (Aug 23) at 9:00 AM Toronto time** — the drip preview and your subscriber modal both confirm it.

## What shipped

**Timezone-aware drip.** The signup form now captures the browser's IANA timezone (`Intl.…().timeZone` — free, no permission prompt; migration 0006 adds `subscribers.timezone`, verified remote). The cron went from daily-13:00-UTC to **hourly**; each pass asks per subscriber: is it their send hour *in their own zone*, and has the cadence elapsed in **local calendar days**? Calendar comparison means a late send never drifts the schedule, and DST comes free via `Intl` (new `LocalTime` module). Unknown zones fall back to the default — America/Toronto, as you chose.

**Everything is a UI setting** (Newsletter → Settings, D1-stored, effective next hourly pass, no deploy): cadence days (2), send hour (9), and default timezone — plus a **per-list override table**: blank inherits the defaults, or give any list its own cadence/hour, with an "effective: every 2d · 9am local" readout per row. The drip now covers **all lists**, each on its own clock; an address on several lists is dripped once, by its first list.

**Ripples kept truthful:** the Drip preview shows list + timezone per subscriber with local-time due slots; the subscriber modal header now reads "one email every 2 days at 9am — America/Toronto" and every projected date in "Coming up" is a real 9:00 AM slot in that person's zone; the welcome email still gates the first post by the cadence.

**A latent bug this exposed:** `Number(null) === 0`, so a *missing* stored setting could pass validation as "hour 0" — midnight sends. Missing rows now read as NaN and fall through to defaults; there's a regression test.

Verification: 114 Worker tests, new dashboard model tests, conventions gate PASS, local E2E 33/33, and live checks of settings, drip preview, and the modal (screenshots taken). That framing holds up under pressure, and I think it's sharper than it first sounds. Let me push on it the way you'd want it pushed.

What people actually *loved* about the Options API was never the `data`/`computed`/`methods` buckets — it was that a component had **anatomy**. You could open a stranger's file and know where everything lived. What killed it was that the anatomy was fake: a plain-object DSL pretending to be a class. `this` was a proxy trick TypeScript fought forever, one logical concern got shredded across three buckets, reuse meant mixins (name collisions, invisible provenance), and none of it existed outside a component.

The Composition API fixed reuse and typing by giving up the anatomy — and setup-soup is the scar tissue. Every team reinvents ordering conventions because the structure the Options API *promised* is gone.

ivue's move is that the anatomy everyone wanted was sitting in the language the whole time: **the class**. And because it's the real thing rather than a DSL imitating it, every fake guarantee becomes a real one — `this` is just `this`, typed natively; a "computed" is a getter, which means it participates in `extends` and `super`, which the Options API never delivered; the buckets come back as *member kinds* (ref-getter = state, plain getter = derived, method = action) but they're prototype members, so they're testable without a mount and usable outside components entirely — the Worker we've been building all week has no components at all and runs the same conventions.

And "beyond it" is measurable, not vibes: the Options API allocated its whole reactive surface per instance; ivue's derivations are prototype getters at zero bytes per instance, and this dashboard is the standing proof — eleven models, a router-backed store, ~167 getters, zero `computed()`.

The honest scoping: ivue didn't defeat the Composition API, it's *built on it* — `ref`, `watch`, composables all work inside the constructor. So the true statement is: it's the Options API's promise, delivered with the Composition API's machinery, exceeding both because the class was the missing structure all along.

I've reviewed it — the invar side is fully mapped. Here's my read, then the recommendation.

## What LazyShared actually closes

It's the last corner of a triangle invar has been fighting for weeks (the `#130` revert-reapply churn, the design-system "per-receiver static-cache caution"):

1. **Per-receiver `$`-caches fork on subclass.** That's the *feature* for memos and per-class tuning — and a silent *bug* for shared stores: a subclass reading `this.$store` quietly gets a fresh registry.
2. The documented fix is a **static field** (one reference on the declaring class, inherited, never receiver-cached) — but an eager field initializer runs **at module load**, so it may only hold dependency-free values. The moment it constructs another namespace's class, you've reintroduced the exact circular-import hazard the whole `$`-getter convention exists to avoid.
3. **LazyShared closes it**: the eager field holds a *cell* (load-safe — a thunk evaluates nothing), the thunk runs on first `.value` read (cycle-safe — every module has loaded), and memoization mutates cell-internal state (fork-safe — no receiver, subclass included, can fork it). Plus the follow-up commit's touch I really like: a self-referential thunk throws a **named, retryable** cycle error instead of a bare stack overflow, and a failed construction doesn't poison the cell.

Honest status on "how invar improved": it landed two days ago with proof-bound specs but **no production call sites yet** — the improvement so far is that a whole trap class (registry forking vs. load-order) went from "caution paragraph" to "universal form the skill can prescribe." That's still real: the skill section now ends in an answer instead of a warning.

## Should it port to ivue extras? Yes — and dropping the namespace pattern is correct, not a compromise

- **It completes ivue's own story.** ivue teaches static `$`-getters as compute-once-per-receiver caches; the shared-store hole is genuinely subtle and we've half-stepped around it ourselves — the dashboard's `AppStore.use()` hides a module-level `let singleton`, which our own *module-level-state* blog post calls a bug class. LazyShared is the principled cell for exactly that, with `reset()` giving test recomposition for free.

That's the precedent that settles your question: the namespace pattern is an **application authoring convention** for classes that grow parents and dependents. LazyShared is a sealed cell — consumers subclassing it is an anti-goal — so `$Class`/`Class` buys nothing, and plain `export class LazyShared<T>` keeps generic inference clean (`new LazyShared(() => new Backend())` infers `T` for free, no `ReactiveInstance` remapping dance).

Four refinements I'd bake into the mandate, because each hides a sharp edge:

1. **Cast to `typeof $X`, not `typeof Class`.** The raw class is where the statics honestly live; `Class = Reactive($Class)` is type-wrapped, and everything else in the pattern (extends, anchors) already points children at `$Class`. So:
   ```ts
   protected get self() {
     return this.constructor as typeof $Box;
   }
   ```

2. **Plain getter, never `$self`.** A `$`-cache would spend a per-instance slot caching something the engine hands you for free — `this.constructor` is a plain property read. As a plain getter it de-optimizes to a native getter: zero bytes, zero indirection.

3. **Subclasses that *add* statics redeclare `self`** with their own `typeof $Sub` — a covariant override, TS accepts it. Inherited as-is, `this.self` is correctly late-bound at runtime (the receiver's class, so per-receiver `$`-caches and overridden statics resolve right), but *typed* as the base. One line per class that needs it; still a ~100:1 reduction.

4. **Keep `self` distinct from the namespace slot — this is the one real trap.** `this.self` is the class you were *constructed from*; `Box.Class` is the *live mutable slot*, which under invar's kernel swapping may be a newer generation. They differ by design. The rule should say it out loud: `this.self` for receiver statics — constants, per-class tuning, `$`-caches; `Namespace.Class` for late-bound capability dispatch. Mandating `self` everywhere would silently pin swap-sensitive reads to a stale generation.

And it composes beautifully with what we just shipped: `this.self.sharedBackend.value` from an instance still converges on the one LazyShared singleton no matter which subclass the receiver is — the fork-proof property survives the sugar.

parts.text: wait, python does the same trick?

Better than that — Python doesn't *do* the trick, Python **is** the trick, baked into the object model. The comparison actually illuminates why JavaScript needs `self` at all:

In Python, an instance attribute lookup that misses falls through to the class, then up the MRO. So a "static constant" is just a class attribute, and `self.TOOLTIP_DWELL_SECONDS` **already works** — no cast, no bridge, late-bound to the receiver's class, subclass overrides honored. When you need the class *object* itself (to construct a sibling, to write a class attribute without shadowing it on the instance), `type(self)` or `cls` in a classmethod hands it to you, also receiver-polymorphic. The whole problem we've been engineering around doesn't exist there.

JavaScript's asymmetry is the culprit: it has **two parallel inheritance chains**. Instance reads walk `instance → prototype → parent prototype`; statics live on a *different* chain, `constructor → superclass`. The chains never touch — `this.X` will never find a static — and the only runtime bridge between them is `this.constructor`, which TypeScript types as bare `Function` because it can't prove which class constructed you. So the cast exists to paper over a type-system gap, and the `self` getter exists to pay for that paper once per class.

Seen that way, the proposal is literally: **re-create Python's unified lookup as a one-line convention.** `this.self.X` is `type(self).X`; the hoisted `const self = this.self` is the classmethod's `cls` in local-variable form. Even the late-binding semantics match — Python's `type(self)` resolves to the subclass exactly like `this.constructor` does, which is why the per-receiver `$`-cache semantics feel natural next to it: Python developers have been living with receiver-polymorphic class attributes forever and it's fine.

It's a good sign for the mandate, honestly — conventions that turn out to be another language's built-in semantics tend to be discovered structure rather than invented style. Same lineage as the blog post from this morning: the anatomy was already in the language; ivue keeps finding the pieces JavaScript scattered.

## Reading your own statics — the ladder

`Reactive(X) === X`, so a namespace's `Class` slot IS the base class. A getter
that reads statics through it therefore hard-binds to the base and silently
IGNORES a subclass override — the exact opposite of what a live (non-`$`)
static getter is for:

```ts
// ❌ three members, a double cast, and the override never applies
protected get Tooltip() {
  return Tooltip.Class as unknown as typeof $Tooltip;
}
public static get TOOLTIP_DWELL_SECONDS() { return 0.4; }
protected get tooltipDwellSeconds() {
  return this.Tooltip.TOOLTIP_DWELL_SECONDS;   // base value forever
}
```

Measured: a subclass setting `0.1` still reads `0.4` through this shape.

Take the first rung that applies:

1. **Nothing outside the instance reads it** → delete the static. A plain
   instance getter is zero bytes per instance and natively overridable:
   ```ts
   protected get tooltipDwellSeconds() { return 0.4; }
   ```
2. **Something outside reads it** (tests pinching the knob, another class)
   → keep the static and read it through **`self`** — the one cast per
   class, declared beside the statics it types:
   ```ts
   protected get self() {
     return this.constructor as typeof $Tooltip;
   }

   protected get tooltipDwellSeconds() {
     return this.self.TOOLTIP_DWELL_SECONDS;
   }
   ```
   `this.constructor` is the actual class — the subclass when subclassed,
   and an engine class that INHERITS `$Class` for a plain reactive
   instance — so statics resolve late-bound in both cases (JavaScript's
   `type(self)`, hand-rolled). TypeScript types `constructor` as bare
   `Function`, so ONE cast is unavoidable; `self` is where it lives.
   Never scatter per-site `(this.constructor as typeof $X)` casts: each
   is an unchecked assertion that the class name is right, and the
   copy-paste error it invites typechecks silently against the wrong
   statics. Rules that keep `self` honest:
   - **Plain getter, never `$self`** — a `$`-cache would spend a
     per-instance slot on what `this.constructor` hands back for free.
   - **One read → `this.self.X` inline. Two or more reads, or any
     loop → hoist:** `const self = this.self;` as the first line, then
     `self.X` throughout. Measured (Node 26): the de-opted `self` getter
     costs ~2 ns/read over an inline cast — noise for a single read —
     while the hoisted form runs at ~0.4 ns/iter in loops, CHEAPER than
     the inline cast, because the engine hoists the class as a loop
     constant.
   - **A subclass that adds statics redeclares `self`** with its own
     `typeof $Sub` (a covariant override); a subclass that only tunes
     inherited statics needs nothing — `self` is already late-bound.
   - **`self` is NOT the namespace slot.** `this.self` is the class you
     were constructed from; `Namespace.Class` is the live mutable slot a
     kernel may have re-pointed since. Receiver statics (constants,
     per-class tuning, `$`-caches) read through `self`; late-bound
     capability dispatch reads through `Namespace.Class`. Blurring them
     trades typo bugs for staleness bugs.
3. **Overriding must NOT happen** → name the class directly,
   `$Tooltip.TOOLTIP_DWELL_SECONDS`, and let the code say so.

Never introduce a `protected get <ClassName>()` self-reference getter. It is a
cast wearing a getter costume: it looks live and is not — `self` is its
honest replacement.

title: Caches, Registries & self
description: Where a class's static values live — per-receiver $-caches, shared static-field registries, LazyShared cells for cross-module construction — and how instance code reads them through self.
---

# Caches, Registries & `self`

A class accumulates static values: memo tables, tuning constants,
registries, shared services. They look alike at the declaration site —
and they are not alike. One of them must fork when the class is
subclassed; another must never fork; a third cannot even be constructed
at the time the file loads. This page is the map: four storage forms,
one read idiom, and the decision that picks between them. The forms are
production-proven — [Invar](/examples/invar)'s 94,000 lines run on
exactly these shapes.

> A static value has one axis that matters: does a subclass get its own
> copy? For a memo, forking is the feature. For a registry, forking is
> the bug.

## The fork trap

`Static()` makes `$`-prefixed static getters
[compute-once-per-receiver caches](/guide/static#cached-static-getters):
the getter body runs once for the base class, and once again for every
subclass that reads it. That is precisely right for memos and per-class
tuning — a subclass that overrides an input derives its own cache
through the override.

Now put a *registry* in one:

```ts
class $CommandRegistry {
  // ❌ looks like a cache, behaves like a fork bomb
  static get $commands() {
    return new Map<string, Command>();
  }

  static register(name: string, command: Command) {
    this.$commands.set(name, command);
  }
}
```

Every receiver gets its own Map. The base class registers ten commands;
a subclass — a test double, a kernel variant, anything that says
`extends` — reads `this.$commands` and receives a **fresh, empty Map**.
Nothing throws. The subclass simply cannot see what the base registered,
and registrations made through the subclass are invisible to everyone
else. The failure is silent, load-order-dependent, and shows up far from
the declaration that caused it.

## Registries: the static field is the pin

A shared store lives in a `static readonly` **field** on the declaring
class. A field is one reference, inherited through the prototype chain,
never receiver-cached — so every access path resolves to the same
object, subclasses included:

```ts
class $CommandRegistry {
  protected static readonly sharedCommands = new Map<string, Command>();

  static get $commands() {
    return this.sharedCommands; // the field IS the pin
  }

  static register(name: string, command: Command) {
    this.$commands.set(name, command);
  }
}
```

The `$`-getter may stay — per-receiver caching over the field is
harmless, because what every receiver caches is the *same reference*.
The field is what guarantees it. This is the form for registries,
ledgers, and any table where "one per process" is the contract.

## The load-order boundary

The static field has one constraint of its own: **its initializer runs
at module load**, while other modules in the import graph may not have
finished loading. A dependency-free value — a bare `new Map()`, a
literal, a `Set` — is always safe. But the moment the initializer
constructs another module's class, it races the import cycle:

```ts
class $SearchRegistry {
  // ❌ runs at module load — SearchBackend's module may not exist yet
  protected static readonly sharedBackend = new SearchBackend.Class();
}
```

This is the same hazard the whole ivue convention exists to avoid —
[cross-module references resolve at first access, never at load
time](/guide/namespace-pattern) — reappearing on the static side. The
instance world solves it with `$`-getters; the static world cannot,
because the `$`-getter forks. Both properties are needed at once:
**load-lazy and unforkable**.

## `LazyShared`: shared and constructed

`LazyShared` (from `ivue/extras`) is the cell that has both properties.
The field eagerly stores the *cell*; the cell holds an inert thunk; the
value construct

  B and B's thunk reads A, the read throws
  `LazyShared thunk cycle: …` instead of a bare stack overflow — the
  message names the repair (break the dependency between the two
  thunks).
- **A throwing thunk never poisons the cell.** Construction that fails
  (a backend not ready, a cycle mid-refactor) leaves the cell
  retryable: the next read runs the thunk again.

The full surface is three members:

| member | role |
| --- | --- |
| `new LazyShared(make)` | store the thunk — nothing evaluates |
| `.value` | construct on first read, memoized thereafter |
| `.reset()` | drop the value; next read constructs again — tests and process recomposition, never production flow |

`.reset()` is the test seam: a spec that needs a fresh shared store
resets the cell instead of reaching into module state.

## Reading your own statics: `self`

The storage forms above are the write side. The read side has a gap of
its own: instance code that reads its class's statics. JavaScript keeps
instance members and static members on two separate inheritance chains,
and the only runtime bridge is `this.constructor` — which TypeScript
types as bare `Function`, forcing a cast at every read.

The standard is one cast per class, named `self`:

```ts
class $Tooltip {
  static get TOOLTIP_DWELL_SECONDS() {
    return 0.4; // live knob — tests and subclasses pinch it
  }

  protected get self() {
    return this.constructor as typeof $Tooltip;
  }

  show() {
    this.dwellTimer.start(this.self.TOOLTIP_DWELL_SECONDS);
  }
}
```

`this.constructor` is the *actual* class — the subclass when subclassed
— so reads are late-bound: a subclass overriding the knob is honored,
and per-receiver `$`-caches resolve through the right receiver. The
cast is declared once, beside the statics it types, instead of asserted
at every call site — where a copy-pasted wrong class name would
typecheck silently against the wrong statics.

Three rules keep `self` sharp:

- **One read → inline; two or more reads, or any loop → hoist.** The
  `self` getter costs ~2 ns per read over an inline cast (measured on
  Node 26, 20 million reads through the production build). Noise for a
  single read — but in loops, hoist it once:
  ```ts
  recalculate() {
    const self = this.self; // one line, one read
    for (const row of this.rows.value) {
      row.height = self.ROW_HEIGHT * self.DENSITY_FACTOR;
    }
  }
  ```
  The hoisted form measures *faster* than inline casts (~0.4 ns per
  iteration vs ~4 ns) — the engine hoists the class as a loop constant.
- **A subclass that adds statics redeclares `self`** with its own
  `typeof $Sub` — a covariant override. A subclass that only tunes
  inherited statics needs nothing; `self` is already late-bound.
- **`self` is not the namespace slot.** `this.self` is the class the
  instance was constructed from; `Namespace.Class` is the live, mutable
  slot a kernel may have re-pointed since. Receiver statics — constants,
  per-class tuning, `$`-caches — read through `self`; late-bound
  capability dispatch reads through the namespace.

An instance getter over a static earns its place when it genuinely
derives — mixing in instance state or transforming the value. A plain
read stays a direct `this.self.X` at the call site, so the knob keeps
one name and one override surface: the static.

## The decision table

| the value is… | form |
| --- | --- |
| a live knob tests or subclasses pinch | non-`$` static getter |
| a memo or per-class tuning — forking on subclass is wanted | `$`-cached static getter |
| a shared registry or ledger, dependency-free to build | `static readonly` field (the pin) |
| shared AND constructs another module's class | `static readonly` field holding a `LazyShared` cell |
| read from instance code | `this.self.X` — hoisted `const self = this.self` in loops |

Every row is the same invariant wearing a different constraint: **one
value, one owner, one override surface** — and construction deferred to
first use, never module load.
